claims.claim: The energy in the sunlight on your skin spent more than a hundred thousand years getting out of the Sun.
claims.source_checked: https://solarscience.msfc.nasa.gov/interior.shtml (NASA MSFC, The Solar Interior, read in full); Crossref metadata api.crossref.org/works/10.1086/172103 and /10.1023/A:1022952621810 (no abstracts); ADS bibcode 1992ApJ...401..759M blocked by a WAF captcha; link.springer.com refused by proxy
claims.note: MSFC: core energy is carried by photons through the radiative zone (25-70% R) and 'an individual photon takes about a million years to finally reach the interface layer'; convection then carries the heat 'quite rapidly' to the surface. So the energy needs on the order of 1e6 years, and 'more than a hundred thousand years' is a true lower bound. The cited papers (Mitalas & Sills 1.7e5 yr, Stix ~3e7 yr) could not be opened, so this confirmation rests on MSFC alone (see claim 19). Suggest adding MSFC's 'about a million years' to SOURCES entry 2, since it is a further published figure inside the stated range.

claims.claim: Hook alone (viewer swipes at second two): the energy reaching you took more than 100,000 years to get out of the Sun.
claims.source_checked: https://solarscience.msfc.nasa.gov/interior.shtml (NASA MSFC, The Solar Interior, read in full)
claims.note: The sentence is about the energy, not the light, so it does not repeat the popular false version ('the light is 100,000 years old'). Taken alone it is true under MSFC's ~1e6-year figure, and under both readings in SOURCES 2.

claims.claim: The trip from the Sun to you took eight minutes.
claims.source_checked: https://physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?c (CODATA 2022: c = 299 792 458 m/s exact); https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/sp330.pdf (NIST SP 330, 2001 ed.: 1 ua = 1.495 978 70(30) x 10^11 m); IAU 2012 B2 PDF not reachable (www.iau.org/static/resolutions/IAU2012_English.pdf is 404; the IAU resolutions page now links to Google Drive, which the proxy refuses)
claims.note: 1.4959787e11 m / 299 792 458 m/s = 499.0 s = 8 min 19 s. 'Eight minutes' is plain rounding (A3). The exact IAU 2012 value could not be opened, but NIST's value agrees with the SOURCES figure to 9 significant digits, which is far more than the claim needs.

claims.claim: Getting out was the slow part.
claims.source_checked: https://solarscience.msfc.nasa.gov/interior.shtml (NASA MSFC, The Solar Interior, read in full) + claim 3
claims.note: Follows from ~1e6 years (MSFC) or >1e5 years against 8.3 minutes. No new number.

claims.claim: But it is not the same light.
claims.source_checked: https://solarscience.msfc.nasa.gov/interior.shtml (NASA MSFC, The Solar Interior, read in full)
claims.note: MSFC: in the radiative zone the energy travels as radiation, 'mostly gamma-rays and x-rays'; at the base of the convection zone the material becomes opaque, 'harder for radiation to get through', and convection carries the heat to the surface, where the energy 'ultimately leaves the surface as visible light' at 5,700 K. So the light leaving is a different kind of light from the radiation inside. Read as 'not the same photons', it rests on claim 6.

claims.source_checked: NASA SVS https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/11084 could not be reached (TLS failure via curl, host not resolvable via WebFetch); https://solarscience.msfc.nasa.gov/interior.shtml (NASA MSFC, The Solar Interior, read in full)
claims.note: The cited support for photon absorption and re-emission (SVS 11084) could not be reached. MSFC does not say it. Its wording ('photons that bounce from particle to particle', 'an individual photon takes about a million years to finally reach the interface layer') reads as one photon crossing the radiative zone, and it says only that radiation finds it 'harder' to get through at 0.7 R, not that none does. 'No photon', with no exceptions, is the author's inference from the hand-off at 0.7 R, which A3 does not allow. To pass: let the session reach svs.gsfc.nasa.gov and confirm SVS says photons are absorbed and re-emitted, or cite a standard textbook on radiative transfer and thermalisation (with edition), or soften to something MSFC does support, such as 'the light that leaves is made near the surface'.

claims.source_checked: https://solarscience.msfc.nasa.gov/interior.shtml (NASA MSFC, The Solar Interior, read in full)
claims.note: More than 1e5 years (MSFC ~1e6 years) of transport supports 'ancient' as a description. Rests on claim 1.

claims.claim: Random-walk path with side-stubs from the centre out to the 0.7 R ring
claims.source_checked: https://solarscience.msfc.nasa.gov/interior.shtml (NASA MSFC, The Solar Interior, read in full)
claims.note: MSFC: energy diffuses outward by radiation through the radiative zone, bouncing from particle to particle. Shown as a schematic random walk, labelled as energy rather than one photon and not to scale.

claims.claim: Path colour shifts linearly with r/R from violet (centre) toward pale yellow (would reach yellow at the surface), so it is about 70% of the way to yellow at 0.7 R
claims.source_checked: https://solarscience.msfc.nasa.gov/interior.shtml (NASA MSFC, The Solar Interior, read in full)
claims.note: Neither MSFC nor SOURCES supports a colour that is linear in radius. MSFC gives 15 MK at the centre, about half that at 0.25 R (7 MK), 2 MK at 0.7 R and 5,700 K at the surface, so temperature is not linear in radius. SOURCES 6 says the radiation at 0.7 R 'is still X-ray'. Yet the path ends 70% of the way to visible-light yellow, which suggests it is mostly softened toward visible light by 0.7 R. On a log-temperature or log-photon-energy scale the radiation is only ~10% of the way at 0.25 R and ~26% at 0.7 R, and the remaining ~74% happens in the convection zone and at the surface. Change: drive the hue from MSFC's temperature profile on a log scale, keeping the path mostly violet up to 0.7 R so the shift to yellow comes at the surface rays; or state in SOURCES 6, and on screen, that the hue is schematic and give the mapping and its reason.
